meta.title_plain: How a manga about a 12-year-old tennis prodigy got kids onto the court
meta.teaser: Takeshi Konomi drew a cocky young tennis star, and real kids grabbed racquets.

page.title: How a manga about a 12-year-old got kids onto the tennis court
page.sub: The story of Takeshi Konomi and The Prince of Tennis
page.bigIdea: Takeshi Konomi kept drawing for six years before his big hit. Then his tennis manga made real kids want to play.

cards.title: Six years to a hit
cards.front: Konomi was born in Japan in 1970. His first manga came out in 1993.
cards.back: His first weekly series started in 1997. His giant hit, The Prince of Tennis, only began in 1999. He kept practising and kept trying.
cards.tryit: Pick one skill you're slow at. Practise it for 10 minutes today, then note one tiny improvement.

cards.title: Meet Ryoma Echizen
cards.front: The hero is a 12-year-old who won four junior tournaments in America in a row.
cards.back: Ryoma moves to Tokyo and joins Seigaku, a school with a strong tennis club. He quickly beats older players and makes the team.
cards.tryit: Draw Ryoma's cap and racquet in a quick sketch. Then draw yourself in your own tennis gear.

cards.title: His own style, not Dad's
cards.front: Ryoma's dad was a famous pro nicknamed "Samurai Nanjiro".
cards.back: Ryoma doesn't just copy his father. Through the story, he invents his own techniques and finds his own style of tennis.
cards.tryit: At practice, copy one shot from a pro. Then add one small twist that makes it yours.

cards.title: Wild shots, real rules
cards.front: Some moves in the series look like black holes or even tennis on horseback.
cards.back: Konomi said he made them wild on purpose to entertain readers and get them talking. But every match still follows the rules of tennis.
cards.tryit: Invent a crazy shot name for your best real shot. Draw a 3-panel comic of you hitting it.

cards.title: Real kids hit the courts
cards.front: By 2003, the show was a huge hit with young fans in Japan.
cards.back: A leader at racquet maker Yonex said Ryoma "is a hero to many of the young generation." He said the show encouraged Japanese kids to play tennis.
cards.tryit: Watch one Prince of Tennis episode. Spot one real tip, like footwork, that you could use.

words.d: Japanese comics, usually read from right to left.
Published one chapter at a time, often every week.
A collected book of manga chapters, like a volume.
A young person with amazing skill at something.
A new story that continues after the first one ends.

quiz.q: Konomi's first manga came out in 1993. How long until The Prince of Tennis began?
quiz.hint: The big hit started in 1999. Do the subtraction.
quiz.why: From 1993 to 1999 is six years of drawing and trying before the hit.

quiz.q: How does Ryoma grow as a player in the story?
quiz.hint: Think about what makes a style truly yours.
quiz.why: Ryoma creates original moves instead of just being a copy of his famous dad.

quiz.q: Konomi's moves look wild. What do the matches still follow?
opts: The rules of a video game
quiz.hint: It's still a tennis manga, even with black holes.
quiz.why: Konomi said the shots are over the top, but everything stays within tennis rules.

quiz.q: What did a Yonex leader say the show did in 2003?
opts: Encouraged Japanese kids to play tennis
quiz.hint: Yonex makes racquets. What would they notice?
quiz.why: He said Ryoma was a hero to young people and the show got kids onto courts.

page.think: Ryoma builds his own style instead of copying his dad. Which part of your tennis could become your own signature move?
